description: Hi! I’m a B.Tech CSE (AI/ML) student from Kerala, India. Our team is tackling the Earth System Trend Detective challenge by building a simple, interactive webpage that uses NASA Earth data to show how a key climate or environmental indicator has changed over time, with clear charts and plain-language insights. Looking for teammates with web development, data visualization or Earth science skills. Beginners welcome!
summary:
Earth System Trend Detective is an interactive webpage that uses NASA data to show how global surface temperature has changed from 1880 to 2025. I developed it with NASA GISS’s GISTEMP v4 record, which gives each year’s temperature compared with the 1951–1980 average. The page shows a “warming stripes” banner with one colored stripe per year, an interactive line chart with a year slider and trend line, and decade-by-decade averages.

It addresses the challenge by finding a clear environmental trend in NASA data: 2024 is the warmest complete year on record, and all ten warmest years fall between 2015 and 2025.

This matters because climate data is often hard for non-experts to read. By turning a 146-year record into simple visuals and plain-language explanations, the project helps students and the public see the warming trend for themselves
details:
Earth System Trend Detective is a single-page interactive website that uses NASA data to show how global surface temperature has changed from 1880 to 2025.

What it does: The page turns NASA’s GISTEMP v4 Land-Ocean Temperature Index (yearly anomalies compared with the 1951–1980 average) into visuals that anyone can read. It has a “warming stripes” banner with one colored stripe per year, an interactive line chart with a year slider and trend line, and decade-by-decade averages. It also computes key findings directly from the data. For example, 2024 is the warmest complete year in the record at +1.28 °C, and all ten of the warmest years fall between 2015 and 2025.

Impact: Climate data is often hard for non-experts to read. This page makes a 146-year NASA record easy to explore, so students and the public can see the long-term warming trend for themselves, and it explains what an anomaly is in plain language.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no external libraries). Charts are drawn with SVG. The data comes from NASA GISS GISTEMP v4 (GLB.Ts+dSST.csv), and the yearly J-D values are used unchanged.

Creative choices: The warming stripes show the trend at a glance before any numbers, and the year slider lets users explore the data themselves. The 2026 data is left out of the charts because the year isn’t finished, and a note explains this.

For the Use of Super Intelligence (SI) box, use this:

I used Claude, an AI assistant from Anthropic, to help write the website’s code (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) and its descriptive text. I chose the challenge, downloaded the NASA dataset, checked the data, tested the page, and published it. The data values are NASA’s own and were not modified by AI. No images, video or audio were AI-generated, and no NASA logos or branding are used.
